title: Alcaraz's 3:34 AM Loss — and the Grin That Said Everything
summary:
Most athletes, after seeing their title defense end at 3:34 in the morning, would not be smiling. Carlos Alcaraz is not most athletes.

After a gruelling four-hour, 28-minute battle against Ben Shelton — the latest finish in US Open history — the 23-year-old Spaniard was filmed walking down the Arthur Ashe tunnel with a huge grin. He had just lost. He looked like he'd won.

Here's why. Alcaraz had been sidelined for over five months with a wrist injury that left him in pain every day. He missed the French Open. He missed Wimbledon. He didn't even know if he'd play in New York until a week before the tournament.

"I suffered, but I enjoyed," he explained. "That's why I smiled when I walked out of the court, because I missed that feeling."

Alcaraz, who has won seven Grand Slam singles titles including this year's Australian Open, wasn't the only player stuck in a late-night marathon. Eventual champion Alexander Zverev finished past 1am in three of his first five matches. Venus Williams wrapped her first-round match at 2am.

"I think it's too much," Alcaraz said of the schedule. "If that match was played earlier, the court could have been packed. I would like to change the schedule a little with a maximum finish at 11pm."

Injuries have hit the sport hard this season. Britain's Jack Draper ended his season early with an arm injury. Alcaraz's rival Jannik Sinner missed the US Open with a knee injury. Alcaraz himself said he'll skip some tournaments in the future to stay "mentally and physically healthy."

This week, he's competing for Team Europe at the Laver Cup in London, captained by Yannick Noah against a World team overseen by Andre Agassi. "When you have your team-mates, the best in the world, by your side, it's a weird feeling but it's beautiful," he said. "We played like our lives depend on it."
why_it_matters: Elite sport is a job like any other, and this story asks who should pay when the schedule eats into athletes' bodies and sleep. That same debate shapes how young players everywhere are trained, rested and protected from injury.

background_read: Carlos Alcaraz is one of tennis's biggest stars — a Spaniard known for his speed, his drop shots and the grin he keeps even when he loses. He has already collected several Grand Slam titles, the four biggest tournaments in the sport.

The US Open is played in New York at the end of every summer, and its night sessions are famous for dragging matches past midnight. Its biggest court, Arthur Ashe Stadium, is named after Arthur Ashe, the American champion who became the first Black man to win a Grand Slam singles title.

The Laver Cup is a three-day team event named after Rod Laver, the Australian legend often described as one of the greatest players ever. It pits Team Europe against Team World, and retired stars such as Yannick Noah (a French former Grand Slam champion) and Andre Agassi (an American former world No. 1) serve as captains — a common second career for great players.

Late-night finishes and a crowded calendar have become a running argument in tennis. Players say a 3 a.m. finish ruins sleep and recovery, while tournaments and television broadcasters point to the money and the drama that night matches create.

perspectives.description: Alcaraz's smile shows a healthy attitude: after five months of daily pain he values simply competing more than protecting a title, and his honesty about suffering makes him a strong role model.

A 3:34 a.m. finish looks like a failure of management — it damages recovery and sleep, and the injuries to Draper and Sinner suggest the calendar asks more of players' bodies than they can safely give.
Night matches are a product. Broadcasters pay for prime-time drama and crowds fill the stands, so tournaments have a financial reason to keep late starts even while players complain.
If top players start skipping events or demanding an 11 p.m. cut-off, Grand Slams may have to shorten formats or start matches earlier — changing the whole rhythm of how the sport is watched.
